investigations__MRI__Brain.front: On which sequence is CSF bright, and what is the mnemonic?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: CSF (water) is bright on T2-weighted imaging. Mnemonic: WW2 = Water is White on T2. On T1, CSF is dark and fat/subacute blood are bright.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What DWI/ADC pattern confirms an acute infarct?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Bright signal on DWI with corresponding LOW (dark) signal on the ADC map = true restricted diffusion. This is the earliest sign of acute infarction, positive within minutes. Bright DWI with a bright ADC is T2 shine-through, not true restriction.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What does FLAIR do and why is it useful?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: FLAIR is a T2 sequence with the CSF signal suppressed (nulled to dark). Suppressing bright CSF lets adjacent periventricular and cortical lesions stand out, making it the workhorse for MS plaques and small ischaemic/gliotic change.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What does enhancement on post-gadolinium T1 indicate?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, allowing contrast to leak into tissue. Seen in tumour, infection and inflammation. A ring-enhancing lesion suggests abscess, glioblastoma or metastasis.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: List the key MRI safety contraindications/hazards.
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Ferromagnetic implants and aneurysm clips, older/non-MR-conditional pacemakers and ICDs, cochlear implants, intra-orbital metallic foreign bodies (projectile/eye injury risk), and loose ferromagnetic objects becoming projectiles. Gadolinium risks nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal impairment (check eGFR).

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: On MRI, what is the classic signal combination of an acute ischaemic infarct on DWI and the ADC map?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: DWI BRIGHT and ADC DARK (low) = true diffusion restriction. This distinguishes a real acute infarct from T2 shine-through (bright DWI but bright/normal ADC).

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Why does acute ischaemia restrict water diffusion?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Failure of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump causes water to shift into cells (cytotoxic oedema). Trapped intracellular water cannot diffuse freely, so DWI signal is retained (bright) and ADC falls (dark), within minutes and before CT changes.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What is the DWI–FLAIR mismatch and why is it clinically useful?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: DWI turns positive within minutes but FLAIR only becomes positive after ~4.5–6 h. A lesion that is DWI positive but FLAIR negative implies onset likely <4.5 h — used to guide thrombolysis in wake-up or unknown-onset stroke.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What is ADC pseudonormalisation and why does it matter?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: The initially low ADC rises back through normal values around days 7–10 (and later becomes high). A subacute infarct can therefore show a falsely 'normal' ADC, so imaging must be interpreted with the timeline in mind.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Before giving thrombolysis in hyperacute stroke, why is CT head (not MRI) done first?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: CT is fast, universally available and reliably excludes intracranial haemorrhage, so reperfusion is not delayed. MRI is slower, has contraindications (pacemaker, metal, unstable patients) and must never hold up a closing therapeutic window.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Name the four typical white-matter locations for MS lesions used in dissemination in space.
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Periventricular, juxtacortical (touching cortex), infratentorial (brainstem/cerebellum), and spinal cord. ≥2 of these satisfy dissemination in space.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What are Dawson fingers and why do they occur?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Ovoid periventricular demyelinating plaques oriented perpendicular to the ventricles/corpus callosum. They follow the deep medullary veins (perivenular inflammation), best seen on sagittal FLAIR.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: How can dissemination in time be shown on a SINGLE MRI scan?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: By the simultaneous presence of a gadolinium-enhancing (active) lesion and a non-enhancing (old) lesion. Otherwise DIT needs a new lesion on a follow-up scan.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What does gadolinium enhancement of an MS lesion indicate, and why?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Active/acute demyelination. Gadolinium leaks in because of blood–brain barrier breakdown; enhancement typically lasts ~2–6 weeks, then the lesion becomes non-enhancing (old).

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What are T1 'black holes' in MS and what do they signify?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Chronic T1-hypointense lesions representing severe demyelination with axonal loss and irreversible tissue damage — a marker of disease chronicity and neurodegeneration (along with brain/cord atrophy).

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Why is gadolinium contrast used in MRI for brain tumours — what does enhancement represent?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Gadolinium cannot cross an intact blood–brain barrier. Enhancement on post-contrast T1 therefore indicates BBB breakdown and/or abnormal tumour neovascularity (leaky vessels). Aggressive lesions (high-grade glioma, metastases, abscess, inflammation) enhance; many low-grade gliomas enhance little or not at all.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: How do you distinguish an extra-axial from an intra-axial lesion on MRI, and give a classic example of each.
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Extra-axial (outside brain): broad dural base, dural tail sign, CSF cleft between lesion and brain, grey–white matter buckled inward — classic is meningioma. Intra-axial (within parenchyma): epicentre in brain, expands cortex/white matter, no CSF cleft — classic is glioma or metastasis.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Give the classic MRI features of a glioblastoma (high-grade glioma).
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Irregular, thick ring enhancement with central necrosis, surrounding vasogenic oedema bright on T2/FLAIR, significant mass effect, and crossing of the midline via the corpus callosum producing the bilateral 'butterfly' appearance. Oedema harbours infiltrating tumour beyond the enhancing rim.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What is the mnemonic for the differential of a ring-enhancing lesion, and which single sequence best identifies an abscess?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: MAGIC DR: Metastasis, Abscess, Glioblastoma, Infarct/Inflammation, Contusion, Demyelination, Radiation necrosis. DWI is key — a cerebral abscess shows central restricted diffusion (bright on DWI, dark on ADC) from viscous pus, whereas most tumours do not restrict centrally.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: An imaging shows a space-occupying lesion with raised ICP. What must you NOT do, and what is initial management?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Do NOT perform a lumbar puncture — risk of coning/herniation from pressure release. Give dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema, monitor and involve critical care if deteriorating, and make an urgent neurosurgical/neuro-oncology referral. Also screen for MRI safety contraindications and check renal function before gadolinium.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What are the specific sequence and orientation used to detect hippocampal sclerosis on an epilepsy-protocol MRI?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: High-resolution, thin-slice coronal T2 and FLAIR oriented perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, allowing side-to-side comparison of the two hippocampi.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What is the classic MRI triad of hippocampal (mesial temporal) sclerosis?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Hippocampal atrophy (volume loss), increased T2/FLAIR signal, and loss of the normal internal architecture. It is the substrate of temporal lobe epilepsy and is potentially surgically curable.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Which structural substrates other than hippocampal sclerosis should an epilepsy-protocol MRI look for?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Focal cortical dysplasia (blurred grey-white junction, transmantle sign), low-grade tumours (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, gliosis/encephalomalacia from prior injury, and malformations of cortical development (e.g. heterotopia, polymicrogyria).

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Why does identifying a lesion on epilepsy-protocol MRI matter clinically?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: In drug-resistant focal epilepsy, finding a discrete resectable focus (e.g. hippocampal sclerosis) enables epilepsy surgery such as anterior temporal lobectomy, offering a potential cure rather than lifelong medication.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Which patients with seizures warrant MRI, and what red flag demands urgent imaging?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Indicated for new focal seizures, focal neurological deficit, atypical features, or established drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Red flag: a first seizure with focal neurology or other red flags may signal a tumour/serious pathology needing urgent imaging. Also give DVLA driving advice and check MRI contraindications.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What atrophy pattern on MRI supports Alzheimer's disease?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Medial temporal lobe / hippocampal atrophy (graded with the Scheltens MTA score on coronal T1) together with parietotemporal atrophy.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: How does the medial temporal lobe help distinguish DLB from Alzheimer's?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: In dementia with Lewy bodies the medial temporal lobe is relatively preserved, whereas in Alzheimer's it is atrophied — so preserved hippocampi favour DLB.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What MRI features suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus, and why does it matter?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy (DESH pattern) with the clinical triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment. It matters because NPH is potentially shunt-responsive (treatable).

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: What does MRI show in vascular cognitive impairment/dementia?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Small-vessel disease: confluent white-matter hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR, lacunes, and strategic infarcts.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: When should dementia prompt urgent imaging for a reversible/serious cause?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Rapidly progressive dementia, focal neurological signs, or young onset — raising suspicion of tumour, NPH, subdural haematoma, or CJD (DWI cortical ribboning).

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Classic MRI distribution of herpes simplex encephalitis?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling of the medial temporal lobes, insula and inferior frontal lobes, with basal ganglia sparing. Often early restricted diffusion, later gyral enhancement and petechial haemorrhage.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Which MRI sequence distinguishes a cerebral abscess from a necrotic tumour, and how?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: DWI. A pyogenic abscess shows CENTRAL restricted diffusion (bright DWI, low ADC) because of viscous pus; a necrotic tumour core usually does NOT restrict (dark DWI, high ADC) and has a thicker, more irregular wall.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: Should you delay aciclovir for MRI or CSF PCR in suspected encephalitis?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: No. Start empirical IV aciclovir immediately — imaging can be normal early and PCR can be falsely negative in the first 24–48 h. Delay increases mortality and disability.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: MRI findings in bacterial meningitis?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Often normal. When abnormal: leptomeningeal enhancement (best on post-contrast FLAIR); MRI mainly detects complications — hydrocephalus, subdural empyema, venous sinus thrombosis, infarcts and early cerebritis/abscess.

investigations__MRI__Brain.front: In an HIV patient with multiple ring-enhancing lesions, what are the two main differentials and the discriminator?
investigations__MRI__Brain.back: Cerebral toxoplasmosis vs primary CNS lymphoma. Toxoplasmosis: multiple lesions favouring basal ganglia/grey–white junction. Lymphoma: tends to be solitary, periventricular, homogeneously enhancing and restricts on DWI (hypercellular).

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Why is MRI (not CT) the imaging test of choice for the posterior fossa?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: The dense petrous/occipital bone causes beam-hardening artefact that degrades CT of the brainstem and cerebellum. MRI has no bone artefact, superior soft-tissue contrast, and DWI detects acute infarcts within minutes — key because posterior circulation strokes are often CT-occult.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: What are the classic paediatric posterior fossa tumours?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Medulloblastoma (midline, off the 4th ventricle roof), pilocytic astrocytoma (cyst with enhancing mural nodule), and ependymoma (arises within the 4th ventricle and extrudes through its foramina — the "plastic" tumour).

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Why is cerebellar haemorrhage a neurosurgical emergency?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: An expanding cerebellar clot compresses the 4th ventricle, causing acute obstructive hydrocephalus and risking tonsillar/upward coning, which can be rapidly fatal. Decompression is considered for clots >3 cm or with brainstem compression/deteriorating GCS.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: How is Chiari I malformation defined on MRI, and what is its key association?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Cerebellar tonsils herniating >5 mm below the foramen magnum (pointed/peg-like on sagittal T1/T2). Key association: a cervical cord syrinx (syringomyelia) — always image the whole spinal cord.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: On MRI, how do you distinguish an epidermoid cyst from an arachnoid cyst at the CPA?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Both follow CSF signal on T1/T2, but an epidermoid shows bright restricted diffusion on DWI, whereas an arachnoid cyst suppresses (follows CSF) on DWI.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: What defines a pituitary microadenoma vs a macroadenoma on MRI, and why does the size cut-off matter?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Microadenoma <10 mm (confined to the sella); macroadenoma ≥10 mm (extends beyond the sella — suprasellar, into cavernous sinus, or inferiorly). The threshold matters because macroadenomas cause mass effect (chiasmal compression, cavernous sinus involvement, hypopituitarism).

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Why is dynamic gadolinium used in pituitary MRI, and how does an adenoma appear?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: The normal gland enhances rapidly, whereas most adenomas enhance more slowly. On early (dynamic) post-contrast images the adenoma therefore appears relatively hypoenhancing (darker) against the briskly enhancing normal gland, improving detection of small microadenomas.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: What visual field defect does a pituitary macroadenoma classically cause, and why?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Bitemporal hemianopia. Upward (suprasellar) growth compresses the optic chiasm, affecting the crossing nasal-retinal fibres that carry the temporal visual fields. It mandates formal visual field testing.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: What is pituitary apoplexy and how does it present?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Sudden haemorrhage or infarction into a pituitary tumour. Presents with abrupt severe (thunderclap-like) headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia (cavernous sinus nerve pressure), and secondary adrenal insufficiency/collapse. It is an emergency needing IV hydrocortisone plus urgent endocrine and neurosurgical input.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Name three non-adenoma sellar/suprasellar lesions and a distinguishing feature of each.
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Rathke cleft cyst — benign non-enhancing cyst, often with an intracystic nodule. Craniopharyngioma — suprasellar, cystic/solid, calcified (especially in children). Empty sella — CSF fills the sella flattening the gland, often incidental. (Craniopharyngioma is the classic calcified paediatric suprasellar mass.)

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for unilateral (asymmetric) sensorineural hearing loss or tinnitus?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: MRI of the internal auditory meatus (IAM) — to exclude a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma). Asymmetric SNHL must never be dismissed as simply age-related.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Which two MRI sequences characterise a vestibular schwannoma and what does each show?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Heavily T2-weighted CISS/FIESTA — the lesion is a filling defect in the bright CSF of the IAM (nerves normally seen as dark strands). Post-gadolinium T1 — the lesion enhances avidly as a bright mass.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: From which structure does a vestibular schwannoma arise, and what is its classic MRI shape?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Schwann cells of the vestibular division of CN VIII, within the IAM. Classic "ice-cream cone" shape when it extends through the porus acusticus into the cerebellopontine angle (cone = IAM tail, scoop = CPA component).

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: What do bilateral vestibular schwannomas indicate?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) — pathognomonic. Always inspect both IAMs, especially in a younger patient.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Name two differentials for a cerebellopontine angle mass and a distinguishing feature of each.
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Meningioma — broad dural base, dural tail, not centred on the IAM. Epidermoid cyst — follows CSF, restricts on DWI, and does NOT enhance. (Vestibular schwannoma is the most common CPA mass.)

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Which MRI sequences are central to imaging the orbit and why?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Fat-suppressed T1/T2 (and STIR) plus post-gadolinium fat-sat T1. Fat suppression darkens the intensely bright orbital fat so that pathological enhancement of the optic nerve or extraocular muscles becomes visible.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Optic neuritis on MRI: appearance and key next investigation?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: A swollen, enhancing optic nerve on fat-suppressed post-gadolinium images. It is strongly linked to multiple sclerosis, so order an MRI brain to look for periventricular demyelinating white-matter lesions.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: How does thyroid eye disease (Graves orbitopathy) appear on MRI, and what is the danger?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Enlargement of the extraocular muscle bellies with sparing of the tendinous insertions (worst in inferior and medial recti). Crowding at the orbital apex risks compressive optic neuropathy.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: Contrast optic nerve glioma vs optic nerve sheath meningioma.
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Optic nerve glioma: children, associated with NF1, fusiform expansion of the nerve itself. Optic nerve sheath meningioma: adults, 'tram-track' enhancement of the sheath around a non-enhancing central nerve.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.front: When is MRI orbits contraindicated, and what is used instead?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.back: Contraindicated with an intra-orbital ferromagnetic foreign body (the field can move it and cause blindness). CT is preferred for acute trauma, bony orbit and to screen for a metal foreign body before MRI.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Why is MRI preferred over CT for local (T) staging of head & neck cancer?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Superior soft-tissue contrast — better shows depth of invasion, perineural spread through skull-base foramina, marrow/cartilage invasion and deep-space (parapharyngeal, tongue-base) extension. CT is better for cortical bone and lung mets.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Which MRI sequence is the 'money' sequence for head & neck tumour and nodal assessment?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Fat-suppressed post-contrast T1 — highlights enhancing tumour, perineural spread and nodal necrosis. DWI/ADC adds cellularity and treatment-response information.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: List MRI features of a malignant cervical lymph node.
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: >1 cm short axis, rounded shape with loss of fatty hilum, central necrosis (non-enhancing core), and extranodal extension (irregular margin/fat stranding). Necrosis and ENE are the most specific.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: When is PET-CT particularly useful in head & neck cancer staging?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Unknown primary (neck node with no obvious source), detection of distant metastases, and post-treatment response assessment (usually ~12 weeks). Complements MRI, which does local T and N staging.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: What is the emergency to recognise in a patient with a large upper-aerodigestive tumour?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Airway compromise/obstruction — stridor. Secure the airway first (senior anaesthetic/ENT input, awake fibreoptic or surgical airway) before any supine imaging.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Where in the nasopharynx does NPC characteristically arise, and which virus is strongly associated?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: It arises in the fossa of Rosenmüller (lateral pharyngeal recess) and is strongly associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV); it is more common in Southeast Asian and southern Chinese populations.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: What is often the FIRST clinical sign of nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: A painless upper cervical neck lump due to cervical/retropharyngeal nodal metastasis — NPC frequently presents with nodal disease before local symptoms.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Why is unilateral serous otitis media in an adult a red flag?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: The tumour obstructs the Eustachian tube, causing unilateral middle-ear effusion and conductive hearing loss. Adult unilateral serous otitis media must prompt nasopharyngeal examination/MRI to exclude NPC.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Why is MRI preferred over CT for NPC staging?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: MRI is superior for soft-tissue contrast and bone-marrow assessment — it better shows depth of invasion, skull-base marrow infiltration, perineural spread, cavernous sinus involvement and retropharyngeal/cervical nodes.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: What is the usual treatment approach for NPC and why?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: NPC is radiosensitive, so management is typically chemoradiotherapy (not primary surgery), coordinated through a head-and-neck MDT after MRI staging and nasendoscopic biopsy.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: What is the relationship between salivary gland size and malignancy risk?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: The smaller the gland, the higher the chance a tumour is malignant. Parotid tumours are mostly benign (~80%), whereas submandibular, sublingual and minor gland tumours carry progressively higher malignancy risk.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Commonest parotid tumour and its classic MRI features?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Pleomorphic adenoma — a well-defined, lobulated, strikingly T2-bright lesion. It is benign but carries a risk of malignant transformation if untreated, so it is excised.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Which salivary malignancy is characterised by perineural spread, and why does MRI matter?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Adenoid cystic carcinoma. MRI is the best modality to trace tumour extension along nerves (e.g. CN VII, V3) toward the skull base, which is essential for staging and surgical planning.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: What does a parotid mass with facial nerve palsy suggest?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Malignant infiltration until proven otherwise. Combined with pain, rapid growth, fixation, or cervical nodes, it is a red flag warranting urgent referral and tissue diagnosis.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Which salivary condition and modality preference applies to stones?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Sialolithiasis (mostly submandibular / Wharton's duct). CT and ultrasound characterise calculi better than MRI; MR sialography can show associated ductal dilatation.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: What is the key MRI strength at the skull base that CT cannot show, and what are its signs?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Perineural tumour spread along cranial nerves through foramina. Signs: loss of normal fat within the foramen, nerve thickening, and abnormal nerve enhancement on fat-suppressed post-gadolinium T1. It upstages the cancer.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Divide skull-base pathology into anterior, central and posterior compartments.
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Anterior (cribriform plate): esthesioneuroblastoma, sinonasal tumours with intracranial spread, CSF rhinorrhoea. Central (sella/clivus): chordoma, chondrosarcoma, pituitary macroadenoma, meningioma; cavernous sinus (CN III–VI + ICA). Posterior (jugular foramen): glomus/paraganglioma ('salt-and-pepper'), schwannoma.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: A destructive midline clival mass, bright on T2 with marrow replacement — what is it?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Chordoma (arises from notochord remnants). An off-midline skull-base cartilaginous tumour at the petro-occipital fissure suggests chondrosarcoma instead.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Describe skull-base osteomyelitis (malignant otitis externa): who, cause, and MRI finding.
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Elderly diabetic with severe otalgia and EAC granulation tissue; usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa spreading from the ear. MRI shows loss of normal bright T1 marrow signal with abnormal bone and soft-tissue enhancement; can cause lower cranial neuropathies. It is an emergency.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Why does normal skull-base marrow appear bright on T1, and why does this matter?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Normal clivus/petrous apex marrow contains fat, which is bright (hyperintense) on T1. Replacement of this bright signal indicates infiltration by tumour or infection (osteomyelitis) — a key early MRI clue.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Why is MRI the best imaging test for TMJ internal derangement?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: It directly images the articular disc — a fibrocartilage structure that is invisible on plain X-ray and CT. MRI also shows joint effusion, marrow oedema and soft-tissue/synovial change.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: What MRI protocol is used for the TMJ and why both positions?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: Oblique sagittal T1/PD (and T2 for fluid) in BOTH closed-mouth and open-mouth positions. Closed mouth shows resting disc position; open mouth shows whether a displaced disc reduces (recaptures).

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Where does the normal articular disc sit on a closed-mouth MRI?
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: It is a low-signal biconcave "bow-tie" with its thick posterior band at the 12 o'clock position over the top of the condyle, and it stays interposed between condyle and eminence during opening.

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Contrast anterior disc displacement WITH vs WITHOUT reduction.
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: WITH reduction: disc is displaced when closed but snaps back onto the condyle on opening — causes clicking. WITHOUT reduction: disc stays displaced on opening — causes limited mouth opening ("closed lock").

investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.front: Name MRI findings in the TMJ beyond disc position.
investigations__MRI__Head & Neck.back: T2-bright joint effusion; degenerative/osteoarthritic change (condylar flattening, osteophytes, subchondral cysts); inflammatory arthritis with synovial thickening and marrow oedema.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Why is whole-spine (rather than regional) MRI used for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Because metastases and cord compression are frequently at multiple, non-contiguous levels and the clinical sensory level often does not match the true compressive level — regional imaging can miss a second, higher lesion that changes management.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: How do vertebral metastases appear on sagittal T1 MRI, and why?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: They appear dark (low signal) because tumour replaces the normal bright fatty marrow of the vertebral body.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What does STIR add to a whole-spine MRI screen?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: STIR suppresses fat, making fluid, marrow oedema and abnormal cord signal bright and conspicuous — good for detecting metastatic deposits, discitis and cord signal change.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What is the emergency management bundle for MSCC?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours, dexamethasone (unless contraindicated), and immediate oncology / spinal surgical referral; treat before neurology becomes irreversible.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: List key MRI safety contraindications to check before a whole-spine scan.
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Non-MRI-conditional pacemaker/ICD, cochlear implant, certain intracranial aneurysm clips, intra-ocular/metallic foreign bodies; also assess renal function before gadolinium and screen for pregnancy and severe claustrophobia.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What is the commonest cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) — chronic cord compression from multilevel spondylosis, disc–osteophyte bars and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy narrowing the cervical canal.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What are the two key MRI hallmarks of degenerative cervical myelopathy?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: (1) Canal stenosis with cord compression and loss of the surrounding CSF collar; (2) high T2 signal within the cord at the compressed level (oedema/myelomalacia), indicating established cord injury.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: How do the clinical signs of DCM distinguish it from cervical radiculopathy?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: DCM causes UMN signs below the level (hyperreflexia, spasticity, upgoing plantars, positive Hoffmann's) with clumsy hands and gait disturbance, possibly LMN signs at the level. Radiculopathy causes dermatomal arm pain and LMN signs in a single myotome with a normal cord.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Why is MRI superior to CT in cervical spine trauma?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: MRI shows the cord itself — contusion/oedema (high T2) — and ligamentous injury, both of which CT cannot demonstrate. It explains neurology that is out of keeping with a normal CT.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What cervical spine complication must be considered in rheumatoid arthritis before GA/intubation?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Atlantoaxial (C1–C2) subluxation from pannus eroding the transverse ligament, risking cord compression at the craniocervical junction — screen with cervical MRI/flexion-extension imaging.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Why is normal vertebral marrow bright on T1, and what does focal T1 low signal in a thoracic vertebra imply?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Adult marrow is fatty, so it is bright on T1 (brighter than disc). Focal or diffuse T1-dark signal means the fat has been replaced — by tumour (metastasis, myeloma), infection or oedema. Marrow replacement is the key MRI sign of malignant vertebral disease.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Describe the MRI cascade of metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC).
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: T1-dark vertebral body deposit → posterior cortical breach → epidural soft-tissue mass → effacement of CSF around the cord → cord compression → high T2 signal within the cord (oedema/myelomalacia). Clinically a sensory level, spastic paraparesis and bladder/bowel dysfunction.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: How does MRI distinguish a benign osteoporotic thoracic compression fracture from a malignant one?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Benign: preserved normal fatty (T1-bright) marrow elsewhere, band-like oedema, posterior fragment retropulsion, spared pedicles, no soft-tissue mass. Malignant: complete T1 marrow replacement of the body, pedicle involvement, convex bulging posterior cortex, epidural/paraspinal mass, other deposits.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: A sensory level on the trunk with spastic legs — where is the lesion and what is the immediate imaging step?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: A sensory level localises to the thoracic cord. This is acute myelopathy / MSCC until proven otherwise — arrange an urgent WHOLE-spine MRI (multiple levels may be involved), not just the symptomatic segment.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Give two intrinsic thoracic cord causes that mimic compression, with their MRI signatures.
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Transverse myelitis — long-segment, central T2 high signal with cord swelling and patchy enhancement. Spinal dural AV fistula — elderly men, diffuse lower thoracic cord oedema with dorsal serpiginous flow voids (treatable, easily missed). (Thoracic disc herniation, often calcified, is a third but is compressive.)

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Where does the spinal cord end, and what lies below that level in the lumbar spine?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: The cord ends at the conus medullaris around L1/L2. Below this there is no cord — only the cauda equina and the exiting nerve roots surrounded by CSF. Compression below L1/L2 causes a cauda equina / root syndrome, not a cord (UMN) syndrome.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Distinguish disc bulge, protrusion and extrusion on MRI.
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Bulge: symmetrical, broad-based extension >25% of the circumference (degenerative, often asymptomatic). Protrusion: focal, base wider than the herniated dome, annulus intact. Extrusion: neck narrower than the herniated material (mushroom), through the annulus; a detached piece = sequestration.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: A paracentral (posterolateral) L4/5 disc herniation compresses which nerve root, and why?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: The TRAVERSING root — L5. Paracentral discs hit the lateral recess where the traversing root (heading to exit one level below) sits medially. By contrast a far-lateral/foraminal L4/5 disc catches the EXITING L4 root.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Contrast the L5 and S1 radiculopathy motor/sensory/reflex picture.
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: L5: sensory loss dorsum of foot & big toe, weak dorsiflexion/big-toe extension (EHL), reflexes normal. S1: sensory loss sole & lateral foot, weak plantarflexion, and a reduced/absent ankle jerk.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: How does neurogenic claudication differ from vascular claudication?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Neurogenic (central canal stenosis): bilateral leg pain on walking/standing, relieved by lumbar flexion/sitting (shopping-trolley sign), pulses present, cycling/uphill tolerated. Vascular: relieved simply by stopping regardless of posture, absent pulses, unaffected by spinal position.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What is the gold-standard, time-critical investigation for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression, and why the whole spine?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: MRI of the WHOLE spine within 24 hours. Metastases are often at multiple levels, so imaging the entire spine avoids missing a second (often silent) compression and guides radiotherapy/surgical planning.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Which primary cancers most commonly cause MSCC, and which spinal region is most often affected?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Breast, lung, prostate, myeloma and renal. The thoracic spine is the commonest site. Mechanism: vertebral body metastasis extends posteriorly into the epidural space and compresses the cord.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Describe the typical clinical sequence of MSCC.
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Progressive back pain first (often nocturnal, worse lying flat or on coughing) → limb weakness → sensory level → LATE bladder/bowel dysfunction. Early back pain is the key warning; sphincter involvement signals poor recovery.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What are the MRI features of MSCC?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Low-T1 marrow-replacing vertebral metastases, an epidural soft-tissue mass indenting the thecal sac, cord displacement/flattening, and high T2 signal within the compressed cord (oedema/myelopathy).

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Outline the immediate management of MSCC.
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Whole-spine MRI within 24 h; immediate high-dose dexamethasone with a PPI; lie flat with spinal precautions until stability known; urgent referral to the MSCC coordinator for surgery vs radiotherapy. Function at treatment predicts outcome, so act fast.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What is the definitive investigation for suspected cauda equina syndrome, and when should it be done?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral (whole) spine — obtained as an emergency, out of hours if necessary. It confirms the compressive lesion and level. Never delay it while waiting for retention to develop.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Why is cauda equina compression a LMN, areflexic pattern rather than UMN?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: The lesion is below the conus (~L1/L2) where the cord has ended, so it compresses peripheral nerve roots (the cauda equina), not the cord — giving flaccid weakness, reduced/absent reflexes, saddle sensory loss and sphincter failure.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Commonest cause of cauda equina syndrome, and the other key differentials?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Commonest: large central disc herniation at L4/5 or L5/S1. Others: tumour (e.g. metastasis), epidural abscess or haematoma, trauma (burst fracture/retropulsed fragment), and severe degenerative canal stenosis.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Distinguish CES-incomplete (CES-I) from CES-retention (CES-R).
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: CES-I: altered urinary sensation / poor stream but voluntary voiding preserved — better prognosis. CES-R: painless retention with overflow incontinence and insensate bladder — worse prognosis. Image and decompress at the CES-I stage before progression to retention.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: Management of confirmed cauda equina syndrome?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Emergency MRI plus immediate spinal surgery referral, then urgent surgical decompression — ideally within 48h of onset and sooner for incomplete CES. Also do a PR exam and post-void bladder scan. Delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What is the gold-standard imaging investigation for suspected spinal infection, and why?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: MRI with gadolinium. It detects discitis/spondylodiscitis and epidural abscess earlier and more sensitively than plain films or CT, defines the extent of infection, and shows any collection compressing the cord or thecal sac.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What is the single most useful MRI discriminator between spinal infection and malignancy?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Infection CROSSES the disc space (endplate-to-endplate involvement of two adjacent vertebrae plus the disc), whereas malignancy tends to SPARE the disc and involves the vertebral body and posterior elements/pedicles.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: List the classic MRI features of pyogenic discitis/spondylodiscitis.
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: T2-hyperintense disc with loss of internal cleft; endplate marrow oedema in the two adjacent vertebrae (low T1, high T2/STIR); erosion/loss of endplate definition; and post-gadolinium enhancement of disc, vertebral bodies and paravertebral tissues.

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: How does spinal TB (Pott's disease) differ from pyogenic discitis on MRI?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: TB predominantly destroys vertebral bodies with RELATIVE DISC SPARING, involves multiple levels with subligamentous spread, forms large paraspinal/psoas 'cold' abscesses, and causes anterior wedge collapse with an angular kyphosis (gibbus deformity).

investigations__MRI__Spine.front: What clinical triad signals a spinal epidural abscess, and what is the management priority?
investigations__MRI__Spine.back: Back pain + fever + neurology (weakness, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction). It is a surgical emergency: urgent whole-spine MRI, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, and emergency decompression/drainage — do not wait for markers or biopsy.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: On MRI, what defines a meniscal tear (rather than degeneration)?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Abnormal linear high signal within the normally dark meniscus that reaches the articular surface (grade 3). Signal not touching a surface is degeneration, not a tear.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What is the "double PCL sign" and what does it indicate?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: A displaced bucket-handle meniscal fragment lies in the intercondylar notch beneath the PCL, mimicking a second PCL on sagittal MRI — a sign of a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which MRI findings are associated with an ACL tear?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Discontinuous/wavy or absent ACL fibres, bone bruising at the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau, anterior tibial translation, and a Segond fracture (lateral tibial rim avulsion).

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What three structures make up the "unhappy triad"?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: ACL + MCL + medial meniscus, torn together after a valgus-plus-rotation force.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: When is MRI indicated in acute knee injury versus X-ray?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Assess clinically first; use Ottawa knee rules to select who needs an X-ray for fracture. MRI is reserved for suspected soft-tissue (meniscal/ligamentous/cartilage) injury or surgical planning, not the first-line acute test.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which rotator cuff tendon is most commonly torn, and why?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Supraspinatus. It passes through the narrow subacromial outlet (prone to impingement) and has a hypovascular 'critical zone' ~1 cm from its greater-tuberosity footprint.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: On MRI, how do you distinguish tendinopathy from a full-thickness cuff tear?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Tendinopathy = increased intratendinous signal with a thickened tendon but NO fluid-signal gap (fibres intact). Full-thickness tear = fluid-signal gap traversing the entire tendon, often with tendon retraction.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which MRI features indicate a chronic / irreparable rotator cuff tear?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Tendon retraction to or medial to the glenoid, and muscle atrophy with fatty infiltration (Goutallier grade on sagittal 'Y' view). Fatty infiltration does not reverse after repair.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What is the imaging investigation of choice for suspected labral tears, and what are a Bankart and a Hill–Sachs lesion?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: MR arthrography (intra-articular gadolinium). Bankart = anteroinferior labral tear after anterior dislocation (bony Bankart if the glenoid rim is fractured); Hill–Sachs = impaction fracture of the posterosuperolateral humeral head.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What is a SLAP tear?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: A Superior Labrum Anterior-to-Posterior tear involving the biceps anchor, typical of overhead athletes or traction injury; MR arthrogram shows contrast undercutting the superior labrum.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Elderly faller, hip pain, cannot weight-bear, but X-ray is normal — next investigation and why?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: MRI (gold standard) to exclude an occult neck of femur fracture. It shows a low-signal fracture line with surrounding marrow oedema (bright on STIR/T2 fat-sat) not visible on plain film. CT is the alternative if MRI is contraindicated/unavailable. Do NOT discharge.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What is the classic MRI sign of avascular necrosis of the femoral head, and where does the lesion sit?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: The "double-line sign" on T2 — an inner bright band (granulation tissue) with an outer dark sclerotic rim — typically in the anterosuperior subchondral femoral head. MRI detects it before X-ray changes or collapse.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: List the classic risk factors for avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Steroids, alcohol excess, sickle cell disease, and trauma (e.g. displaced femoral neck fracture disrupting retinacular vessels). Others include SLE, radiotherapy, and dysbarism/caisson disease.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: How does MRI distinguish transient osteoporosis of the hip from AVN?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Transient osteoporosis shows diffuse marrow oedema of the head and neck but NO double-line sign and NO subchondral fracture; it is self-limiting (often middle-aged men or 3rd-trimester pregnancy). AVN shows a focal subchondral lesion with the double-line sign and risk of collapse.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which imaging is used for suspected labral tear / femoroacetabular impingement, and what are the two FAI morphologies?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: MR arthrography (intra-articular contrast) best demonstrates acetabular labral tears. FAI types: cam (femoral head-neck junction bump) and pincer (acetabular over-coverage); the two often coexist (mixed).

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: On MRI, how does Achilles tendinopathy differ from a full-thickness rupture?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Tendinopathy = fusiform thickening with increased intrasubstance signal but intact fibres. Full-thickness rupture = complete fibre discontinuity with a fluid-filled gap and retracted wavy ends (positive Simmonds/Thompson test clinically).

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which MRI features favour osteomyelitis over Charcot arthropathy in the diabetic foot?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Osteomyelitis: marrow signal REPLACEMENT (low T1, high T2/STIR, enhancement) usually in a single bone with an ADJACENT skin ulcer or sinus tract. Charcot: joint-centred MIDFOOT deformity/fragmentation (rocker-bottom), no ulcer/sinus tract.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What normal MRI marrow finding is lost in bone infiltration or osteomyelitis, and on which sequence?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Normal marrow is bright on T1 because of its fat content. Loss/replacement of this bright T1 marrow signal is the red flag for infiltration or osteomyelitis.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which ankle ligament is most commonly injured, and what is the classic cause of adult acquired flatfoot on MRI?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: The ATFL (then CFL) is most commonly injured after an inversion sprain. Adult acquired flatfoot is classically due to tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction (degeneration/tear of the tendon medial to the malleolus).

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Name two high-risk stress fracture sites in the foot best detected by MRI and the tell-tale MRI finding.
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: The tarsal navicular (prone to non-union) and the metatarsals (2nd/3rd 'march' fracture). MRI shows marrow oedema (bright on STIR) with a low-signal fracture line before radiographs turn positive.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What is the single classic indication for MRI wrist in a trauma patient?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: A clinically suspected scaphoid fracture (FOOSH with anatomical snuffbox tenderness) when the initial X-ray is normal. MRI is the gold-standard test to detect the occult fracture early via the fracture line and bone-marrow oedema.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Why does a missed scaphoid waist/proximal-pole fracture cause avascular necrosis?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters distally). A waist or proximal-pole fracture cuts off the proximal fragment's supply, leading to AVN and non-union (SNAC wrist).

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: What MRI signal changes indicate an acute scaphoid fracture?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: A low-signal (dark) fracture line on T1 crossing the bright fatty marrow, plus high-signal (bright) bone-marrow oedema on T2/STIR fat-suppressed sequences.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which non-fracture wrist pathologies is MRI used to diagnose?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: TFCC tears (ulnar-sided wrist pain), scapholunate ligament tears (instability/SLAC wrist), Kienbock's disease (lunate AVN), ganglion cysts, and tendon pathology such as de Quervain's tenosynovitis.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Name key MRI safety contraindications to screen for before a wrist scan.
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Cardiac pacemakers, cochlear implants, metallic intra-ocular/orbital foreign bodies (metalworkers), and certain aneurysm clips or implants. Check MR-conditional status; caution with gadolinium in significant renal impairment. MRI uses no ionising radiation.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow") — which structure, and MRI features?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Degeneration/tear of the COMMON EXTENSOR ORIGIN, chiefly ECRB. MRI: tendon thickening with increased signal on fluid-sensitive sequences; fluid-signal cleft or fibre discontinuity indicates a tear that may extend into the LCL.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which elbow ligament is injured in throwing athletes, and what is the best MRI test?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: The ULNAR (medial) COLLATERAL LIGAMENT — primary restraint to valgus stress. Fails in pitchers/overhead athletes causing valgus instability. MR arthrography is most sensitive; contrast tracking under a partial distal tear gives the "T sign".

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Distal biceps tendon rupture — clinical signs and why MRI matters?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: Weak SUPINATION and flexion, retracted "reverse Popeye" belly, palpable gap; inserts at the radial tuberosity. MRI (FABS view) distinguishes COMPLETE vs PARTIAL and measures retraction — the key determinant for prompt surgical repair.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Which nerve is entrapped at the cubital tunnel, and what does MRI show?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: The ULNAR NERVE, behind the medial epicondyle — cubital tunnel syndrome (2nd commonest entrapment neuropathy). MRI: thickened, T2-bright/oedematous nerve, sometimes subluxation over the epicondyle.

investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.front: Capitellar osteochondritis dissecans — who gets it, and what does an X-ray fat-pad sign suggest in an adult?
investigations__MRI__Musculoskeletal — J.back: OCD of the capitellum affects adolescent throwers and gymnasts; MRI grades stability and detects loose bodies (Panner disease is the younger self-limiting mimic). A posterior fat-pad sign / raised anterior sail sign in an adult implies an occult radial head fracture.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: Why is MRI uniquely sensitive to bone marrow pathology?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: It images marrow fat and water directly. Normal adult (yellow) marrow is fatty and bright on T1; almost any pathology replaces fat with water or cells, giving the universal signature of LOW T1 and HIGH T2/STIR. STIR (fat-suppressed) makes oedema/infiltration most conspicuous.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: How does an occult fracture appear on MRI, and give three classic sites where X-ray is often normal.
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: A fracture line dark on all sequences, surrounded by marrow oedema (low T1, high STIR), visible days before X-ray changes. Classic occult sites: scaphoid (post-FOOSH), femoral neck/hip (elderly faller), and sacral insufficiency fractures (osteoporotic/elderly).

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: What is the double-line sign and what does it indicate?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: A T2 finding of avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis): an inner BRIGHT line of hypervascular granulation tissue and an outer DARK line of reactive sclerosis demarcating the necrotic segment. MRI detects AVN pre-collapse, before X-ray. Classic site: femoral head.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: List the major risk factors for avascular necrosis.
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Steroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, and trauma are the classic four. Others: SLE, dysbaric/decompression (the bends), radiotherapy, and Gaucher disease.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: How do metastases and myeloma appear in marrow on MRI, and what internal control confirms replacement?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: They replace bright fatty marrow and appear DARK on T1 (focal deposits or diffuse disease); whole-body STIR is standard for myeloma staging/skeletal screening. Internal control: normal adult marrow should be brighter than muscle and brighter than the intervertebral disc on T1 — marrow darker than disc suggests replacement/infiltration.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: Why can a plain X-ray be normal in early osteomyelitis, and what is the imaging of choice?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Bone destruction needs ~30–50% mineral loss to be visible, giving a ~2-week (10–14 day) lag. MRI with gadolinium is the most sensitive and specific test — it detects marrow oedema within days.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: What is the most specific MRI sign of osteomyelitis, and on which sequence?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Confluent marrow signal REPLACEMENT: low signal on T1 (replacing normal bright fatty marrow), with high T2/STIR and post-gadolinium enhancement. Confluent low-T1 marrow is the most specific pattern.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: Define sequestrum and involucrum in chronic osteomyelitis and their MRI behaviour.
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Sequestrum = a fragment of dead avascular bone, low signal on all sequences and NON-enhancing (nidus for relapse, needs surgery). Involucrum = shell of new living bone around it, which DOES enhance.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: How does MRI distinguish a soft-tissue abscess from cellulitis?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Abscess = rim-enhancing fluid collection with a non-enhancing centre and restricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC) — drainable. Cellulitis = reticulated (lace-like) subcutaneous oedema with diffuse enhancement and NO drainable collection.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: A patient has severe pain out of proportion to skin findings, systemic toxicity and crepitus. What is the diagnosis and management, and what is the role of MRI?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Necrotising fasciitis — a CLINICAL diagnosis and surgical emergency. Immediate surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics; do NOT delay for MRI. (MRI, if done, shows fluid/oedema and enhancement along deep fascia, with gas.)

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: Why is MRI the imaging modality of choice for a suspected soft-tissue sarcoma?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Superior soft-tissue contrast lets it characterise the mass and locally stage it — defining size, compartment, and the relationship to the neurovascular bundle and bone for surgical planning. It cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant on signal alone.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: List the red-flag features of a soft-tissue lump warranting urgent MRI and sarcoma-unit referral (2-week-wait criteria).
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Size >5 cm, deep to fascia, rapidly growing, painful, or recurrent. Any of these = sarcoma until proven otherwise.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: Why must an unknown soft-tissue mass never be excised before imaging and biopsy?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: An unplanned "whoops" excision seeds tumour and worsens outcomes. The mass needs MRI plus an MDT-planned image-guided core biopsy placed along the future resection line, so the biopsy tract can be excised en bloc.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: How does a lipoma and a GCT of the tendon sheath (PVNS) each appear on MRI?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Lipoma follows fat on all sequences (bright on T1, suppresses on fat-sat). GCT of tendon sheath / PVNS contains haemosiderin causing low signal and "blooming" artefact on gradient-echo (GRE) sequences.

investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.front: How is a soft-tissue sarcoma staged, and where does it metastasise?
investigations__MRI__MSK — Bone & Soft T.back: Local staging with MRI of the primary; distant staging with CT chest. Sarcomas spread haematogenously, characteristically to the lungs.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 68-year-old presents with sudden right-sided weakness 40 minutes ago. CT head shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. Which MRI sequence would most sensitively confirm an acute ischaemic stroke at this early stage?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with ADC map
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: DWI is the earliest and most sensitive sequence for acute infarction, showing restricted diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC) within minutes, long before CT or conventional T1/T2 changes appear. GRE detects blood, and post-gadolinium T1 detects BBB breakdown, neither of which is the earliest stroke sign.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: On an axial brain MRI, the CSF within the lateral ventricles appears bright (high signal) and periventricular white matter lesions are conspicuous, while the CSF signal has been nulled on a companion image. Which pair of sequences is being described?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: T2 and FLAIR
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Bright CSF indicates a T2-weighted image (Water is White on T2). FLAIR is a T2 sequence with the CSF signal suppressed (nulled) so periventricular lesions stand out. The described combination of bright-CSF T2 plus a CSF-suppressed companion is therefore T2 and FLAIR.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient is referred for a routine brain MRI. Which finding in the safety screening should most strongly prompt further investigation before entering the scanner?
options: A history of metal grinding with possible retained intra-orbital metallic fragment
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: A history of metal grinding with possible retained intra-orbital metallic fragment
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: A ferromagnetic intra-orbital foreign body can move within the strong magnetic field and cause globe injury or blindness, so a grinding/metalwork history mandates screening imaging (e.g. orbital radiographs) before MRI. Titanium is non-ferromagnetic and MR-safe; the other options are not MRI hazards.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 68-year-old presents 90 minutes after sudden right-sided weakness and dysphasia. MRI shows a wedge of high signal on DWI in the left hemisphere. Which finding on the ADC map confirms this is TRUE acute diffusion restriction rather than T2 shine-through?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Low (dark) signal on ADC
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: True acute restriction is DWI bright WITH ADC dark (low). If the ADC were bright/normal, the DWI signal would represent T2 shine-through, not acute cytotoxic restriction. GRE blooming indicates haemorrhage and ring enhancement suggests abscess/tumour.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient wakes with a hemiparesis and cannot say when symptoms began. MRI shows a lesion that is DWI positive but FLAIR negative. What does this DWI–FLAIR mismatch most likely indicate?
options: The stroke is more than 24 hours old
The lesion is a chronic infarct
The stroke onset is likely within the last 4.5 hours
The lesion represents a tumour rather than infarct
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: The stroke onset is likely within the last 4.5 hours
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: DWI turns positive within minutes while FLAIR lags ~4.5–6 h. DWI+/FLAIR− (mismatch) implies onset is probably <4.5 h, supporting thrombolysis in wake-up or unknown-onset stroke.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which statement about MRI in the hyperacute stroke pathway is CORRECT?
options: MRI should always be performed before CT to save time
A non-contrast CT head is done first to exclude haemorrhage so reperfusion is not delayed
DWI is unable to detect posterior fossa infarcts
GRE/SWI sequences are insensitive to haemorrhage
ADC remains low permanently after infarction
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: A non-contrast CT head is done first to exclude haemorrhage so reperfusion is not delayed
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: CT is fast and universally available and reliably excludes haemorrhage before thrombolysis; MRI must not delay time-critical reperfusion. DWI is in fact superior for posterior fossa infarcts, GRE/SWI are highly sensitive to blood, and ADC pseudonormalises over days.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A DWI-restricting lesion is seen but the clinical picture is atypical for stroke (fever, no vascular territory pattern). Which of the following is a recognised NON-stroke cause of diffusion restriction?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Cerebral abscess
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Central pus in a cerebral abscess restricts diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC) and shows a ring-enhancing wall; hypercellular tumours (lymphoma, high-grade glioma) can also restrict. These mimics are why lesion shape, enhancement pattern and clinical context matter, not DWI alone.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient has sudden vertigo, ataxia and diplopia; CT brain is reported as normal. Why is MRI-DWI particularly valuable here?
options: CT is more sensitive than MRI for posterior fossa infarcts
MRI-DWI detects small brainstem/cerebellar infarcts that CT often misses due to bone artefact
DWI cannot image the posterior circulation
FLAIR is positive before DWI in the brainstem
MRI is contraindicated in posterior circulation stroke
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: MRI-DWI detects small brainstem/cerebellar infarcts that CT often misses due to bone artefact
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: CT of the posterior fossa is degraded by beam-hardening/bone artefact, so small brainstem and cerebellar infarcts are frequently missed. DWI is highly sensitive there, making it the test of choice for posterior circulation symptoms with a normal CT.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 29-year-old woman has an episode of painful visual loss in one eye that recovered. MRI brain FLAIR shows several ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the corpus callosum, plus a juxtacortical lesion. Post-gadolinium imaging shows one lesion enhances while the others do not. Which statement best explains why MS can be diagnosed from this single scan?
options: Optic neuritis alone is diagnostic of MS
The perpendicular orientation of lesions is pathognomonic and sufficient
Simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions satisfy dissemination in time, and ≥2 typical sites satisfy dissemination in space
Any white-matter lesion on FLAIR confirms demyelination
Enhancement excludes MS because it indicates infection
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions satisfy dissemination in time, and ≥2 typical sites satisfy dissemination in space
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: McDonald criteria require dissemination in space (≥2 of the four typical locations — here periventricular + juxtacortical) and in time. An enhancing lesion coexisting with a non-enhancing lesion demonstrates lesions of differing age on one scan, satisfying DIT without a follow-up study.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which MRI feature would most strongly suggest an alternative diagnosis rather than typical multiple sclerosis?
options: Ovoid periventricular lesions on sagittal FLAIR
A longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion spanning several vertebral segments
A juxtacortical lesion touching the cortex
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: A longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion spanning several vertebral segments
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: MS cord lesions are characteristically short (<2 vertebral bodies) and peripheral. A longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis lesion points instead to neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin-4 antibody), a red flag against typical MS. The other features are all typical of MS.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: What does gadolinium enhancement of a white-matter plaque on T1 imaging indicate in multiple sclerosis?
options: Active demyelination with blood–brain barrier breakdown
An artefact from CSF suppression on FLAIR
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Active demyelination with blood–brain barrier breakdown
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Gadolinium cannot cross an intact blood–brain barrier. In acute demyelination the BBB is disrupted, allowing contrast to leak into the lesion, so enhancement marks an active/acute plaque (usually for ~2–6 weeks). Non-enhancing lesions are old; black holes reflect chronic axonal loss.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 58-year-old presents with headache and left-arm weakness. MRI+gadolinium shows a solitary intra-axial mass with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis and extensive surrounding T2/FLAIR oedema, crossing the corpus callosum to the contralateral hemisphere. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Glioblastoma
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Thick irregular ring enhancement with central necrosis, marked vasogenic oedema and midline crossing through the corpus callosum (butterfly appearance) is the classic pattern of glioblastoma. Meningioma is extra-axial with a dural tail; an abscess would show a thin smooth ring with central restricted diffusion; infarct follows a vascular territory; tumefactive MS classically shows an open (incomplete) enhancing ring.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A ring-enhancing lesion is seen on MRI. On diffusion-weighted imaging the centre of the lesion shows marked restricted diffusion (bright on DWI, low ADC). Which diagnosis does this most strongly suggest?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Cerebral abscess
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Central restricted diffusion within a ring-enhancing lesion reflects viscous, cellular pus and is the classic feature of a cerebral abscess. Most necrotic tumours (glioblastoma, metastasis) have a non-restricting central cavity. This single sequence critically changes management from biopsy/resection to antibiotics and neurosurgical drainage.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: An MRI shows a well-defined, homogeneously enhancing extra-axial mass with a broad dural base, a dural tail sign and a CSF cleft separating it from the brain. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Meningioma
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: A broad dural base, dural tail sign, CSF cleft and homogeneous avid enhancement are hallmark features of an extra-axial meningioma. Metastases and gliomas are intra-axial (within brain parenchyma) and lack a CSF cleft; an abscess shows a ring with central restricted diffusion. Identifying the extra-axial location first narrows the differential decisively.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 24-year-old with drug-resistant seizures and rising epigastric aura undergoes an epilepsy-protocol MRI. Coronal FLAIR shows a small right hippocampus with high signal and loss of internal architecture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Hippocampal (mesial temporal) sclerosis
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Hippocampal atrophy, increased T2/FLAIR signal and loss of internal architecture are the diagnostic triad of hippocampal sclerosis, the commonest substrate of temporal lobe epilepsy and one that is potentially curable with anterior temporal lobectomy. The other options are alternative substrates but do not produce this hippocampal triad.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which sequence and orientation is most important for detecting the commonest surgically-treatable substrate in an epilepsy-protocol MRI?
options: Axial diffusion-weighted imaging through the whole brain
Sagittal T1 volumetric sequence of the midline
Coronal T2/FLAIR angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus
Post-contrast axial T1 of the posterior fossa
Gradient-echo axial imaging of the basal ganglia
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Coronal T2/FLAIR angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Thin-slice coronal T2/FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus allows direct side-to-side comparison and reveals the atrophy and signal change of hippocampal sclerosis that routine axial imaging often misses. The other sequences do not optimally interrogate the mesial temporal structures.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A previously well 55-year-old has a first focal seizure and is found to have a new right-sided pronator drift. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and arrange routine outpatient EEG only
Start lifelong sodium valproate without imaging
Arrange urgent neuroimaging to exclude a structural lesion such as a tumour
Discharge with no follow-up as most first seizures are benign
Repeat clinical review in six months before any investigation
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Arrange urgent neuroimaging to exclude a structural lesion such as a tumour
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: A first seizure with a focal neurological deficit is a red flag that may indicate an underlying tumour or other serious structural pathology, so urgent imaging is required rather than reassurance. Driving advice (stop driving, notify the DVLA) and screening for MRI contraindications should also be addressed.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 72-year-old presents with 18 months of memory decline. Coronal T1 MRI shows bilateral medial temporal lobe atrophy with a high Scheltens MTA score and parietotemporal volume loss. Which diagnosis does this best support?
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Alzheimer's disease
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Hippocampal/medial temporal lobe atrophy (high MTA score) with parietotemporal involvement is the classic Alzheimer's signature. FTD gives asymmetric frontal/anterior temporal atrophy, DLB relatively spares the medial temporal lobe, NPH shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, and vascular dementia shows small-vessel disease.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 68-year-old has a gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline. MRI shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to cortical atrophy with tight high-convexity sulci. What is the most important reason to recognise this pattern?
options: It indicates a potentially shunt-responsive condition
It is diagnostic of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: It indicates a potentially shunt-responsive condition
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: The triad plus ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy (DESH pattern) is normal pressure hydrocephalus, a treatable/reversible cause of dementia that may respond to CSF shunting — hence the importance of not missing it. CJD is suggested by DWI cortical ribboning, not this pattern.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 59-year-old develops rapidly progressive cognitive decline over weeks with myoclonus. Which MRI sequence and finding would most support Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
options: DWI showing cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restricted diffusion
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: DWI showing cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restricted diffusion
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Rapidly progressive dementia should trigger urgent imaging for reversible/serious causes; in CJD, DWI classically shows restricted diffusion as cortical ribboning and in the basal ganglia. Hippocampal atrophy suggests AD, confluent white-matter change suggests small-vessel disease, and microbleeds relate to amyloid/hypertensive angiopathy.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A 34-year-old presents with fever, confusion and expressive dysphasia. MRI shows asymmetric FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling of the left medial temporal lobe and insula, sparing the basal ganglia. What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Await CSF HSV PCR before starting any treatment
Arrange urgent CT angiogram for stroke thrombolysis
Start IV dexamethasone alone and observe
Repeat MRI in 48 hours to confirm progression
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Start empirical IV aciclovir immediately
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: The pattern is classic for HSV encephalitis. Treatment is time-critical and must not wait for PCR or repeat imaging — empirical IV aciclovir is started at once. PCR can be falsely negative early, and delay worsens outcome. Basal ganglia sparing helps distinguish it from MCA infarction, so thrombolysis is inappropriate.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient has a ring-enhancing cerebral lesion with surrounding oedema. Which single MRI feature best supports a pyogenic abscess over a necrotic high-grade tumour?
options: Central restricted diffusion (bright DWI, low ADC)
A thick, irregular, nodular enhancing wall
Facilitated diffusion in the lesion centre
Homogeneous enhancement of the whole lesion
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Central restricted diffusion (bright DWI, low ADC)
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Viscous pus in an abscess restricts diffusion centrally — bright on DWI with low ADC — whereas a necrotic tumour core typically does not restrict (facilitated diffusion, high ADC) and has a thicker, more irregular wall. Both may show oedema, so that is not discriminatory.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: A patient with suspected bacterial meningitis has a new focal neurological deficit and reduced GCS. What is the correct sequence of management?
options: Perform lumbar puncture first, then treat based on results
Take blood cultures and give antibiotics, then image before LP
Delay all antibiotics until MRI and LP are both complete
Perform LP immediately regardless of the focal signs
Give antibiotics only after LP confirms bacterial cause
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Take blood cultures and give antibiotics, then image before LP
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: Focal deficit, depressed GCS, seizures or signs of raised ICP require imaging before LP to exclude a mass lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus and the risk of coning. However, this must never delay empirical treatment — take blood cultures and give antibiotics (plus aciclovir if encephalitis is possible) first, then image, then LP if safe.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Which MRI finding is most characteristic of CNS tuberculosis?
options: Bilateral non-haemorrhagic medial temporal signal only
Basal leptomeningeal enhancement with tuberculomas and hydrocephalus
Central restricted diffusion in a thin-walled cystic lesion
Isolated gyral petechial haemorrhage of the frontal lobes
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Basal leptomeningeal enhancement with tuberculomas and hydrocephalus
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: TB meningitis characteristically produces thick basal leptomeningeal enhancement, parenchymal tuberculomas (ring or nodular enhancing), communicating hydrocephalus and infarcts from associated vasculitis. Bilateral medial temporal signal suggests autoimmune/HSV encephalitis; a solitary periventricular enhancing mass suggests lymphoma.

investigations__MRI__Brain.question: Before an urgent contrast-enhanced MRI brain for suspected CNS infection, which factor is the most important routine safety check?
options: Screening for pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants/foreign bodies
Confirming the patient has fasted for 12 hours
Ensuring the patient can lie prone for the scan
Verifying a normal chest radiograph first
investigations__MRI__Brain.answer: Screening for pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants/foreign bodies
investigations__MRI__Brain.explanation: MRI safety screening for ferromagnetic and electronic implants (pacemakers, cochlear implants, metallic foreign bodies) is mandatory because the static magnetic field can cause device malfunction or projectile injury. Gadolinium is weighed against renal function (eGFR), not sodium, and fasting/prone positioning are not routine requirements.

investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.question: A 68-year-old man develops sudden vertigo, gait ataxia and vomiting. Non-contrast CT head is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
investigations__MRI__Skull Base & Specia.explanation: Posterior circulation (cerebellar) strokes are frequently missed on early CT due to bone beam-hardening artefact and small lesion size.
